## Project summary

Core 4x4 is a real-business analytics project centered on marketplace and internal sales data arriving in different export formats. The repository implements a local Windows application that turns those inputs into a standardized, traceable event ledger.

The workflow supports file-type detection, product and SKU mapping, exact-file and business-record duplicate handling, validation reports, optional SQL Server loading, and analytics views for Power BI. Proprietary records and business details are intentionally excluded from this public case study.

## Business problem

Sales information from separate platforms can differ in structure, naming conventions, product identifiers, and record quality. Without a consistent preparation process, those differences make it harder to combine records and use them reliably in reporting.

The project addresses the need for a shared analytical foundation: one that preserves the useful information in each source while applying common business rules before analysis.

## My approach

I approached the project as a data reliability problem rather than a simple file-conversion task. I reviewed source structures, built Python transformation and identity logic, defined validation behavior, implemented approved product and SKU mapping, and prepared SQL and Power BI assets around the resulting event ledger.

Specific organizational details, credentials, and proprietary records are intentionally omitted.

## Architecture

The application separates source adapters, a canonical event schema, shared validation and mapping rules, batch orchestration, and controlled delivery steps. Users can process files through a local desktop or browser interface, review warnings, save a standardized CSV and validation report, and optionally load an approved result into SQL Server for Power BI.

::: {.solution-callout}
### Design principle

Separate source-specific cleanup from shared business rules. This makes the workflow easier to reason about and extend when a source changes or a new one is introduced.
:::

## Key technical decisions

:::: {.challenge-grid}
::: {.challenge-card}
### Preserve event meaning
The canonical schema keeps `record_type` separate from row grain so order lines and standalone financial events—such as fees, payouts, holds, and refunds—are not forced into the same meaning.
:::

::: {.challenge-card}
### Separate identity levels
The pipeline uses a file hash for exact uploaded bytes and a business `record_key` for cross-file deduplication. Those identifiers answer different questions and remain separate.
:::

::: {.challenge-card}
### Keep legitimate repeats
Rows with the same logical identity receive occurrence-aware record keys in source order. Repeated real events remain distinct, while a harmlessly resaved report reproduces the same sequence of keys.
:::

::: {.challenge-card}
### Control mapping
Only explicitly approved SKU mappings populate the standardized SKU. Suggested, missing, or conflicting mappings remain visible for review instead of being silently accepted.
:::
::::

## Data quality and validation

Source detection uses report-column signatures rather than filenames. Unsupported or uncertain files require manual source selection, and questionable rows are preserved with either `warning` or `review_needed` status instead of being silently discarded.

The output retains provenance fields for the import run, source file, system, report, row number, and adapter version. Automated tests cover schema consistency, long text identifiers, duplicate files, cross-file business duplicates, occurrence-aware record identity, approved mapping behavior, SQL contracts, and Power BI assets. Database integration tests are available separately when SQL Server is configured.

## Key capabilities

- Source adapters for tested eBay and Core 4x4 exports
- Automatic source detection with a manual selection fallback
- Canonical event ledger with source lineage and occurrence-aware record keys
- Approved SKU mapping from XLSX or CSV files
- Exact-file and business-record duplicate handling
- Validation reports with warning and review-needed records
- Transactional SQL Server loading for approved runs
- Purpose-specific SQL analytics views and documented Power BI measures
- Provisional Amazon adapter that remains unvalidated without a representative sample

## Business value

The pipeline provides a consistent foundation for sales analysis by making source differences, lineage, mapping rules, duplicate handling, and validation explicit parts of a repeatable process. Analysts can review file and record outcomes before an approved run is stored for downstream reporting.

No quantitative performance or financial claims are included because those outcomes have not been established for publication.

## What I learned

This project reinforced that dependable analytics begins before a dashboard is built. Source context, naming conventions, product identity, and validation rules all shape whether an analytical output can be trusted.

It also highlighted the importance of designing workflows in stages. A modular process makes it easier to isolate issues, revise business rules, and communicate how raw information becomes a reporting dataset.

## Future improvements

The repository identifies real-sample Amazon validation, cross-source order reconciliation, and continued operational hardening as future work. Amazon support remains provisional until representative exports pass the same detection, transformation, and validation checks as the tested sources.
